schools.summary: Matthew Henry turns the heading into a second exodus: Ezra sets up an ensign to gather the outcasts (Isa. 11:12); the willing volunteers, 1496 males, are named house by house for their honour, some coming early and some late yet none rejected.
Ellicott reads the register form — heads of houses followed by their wider families — and compares the roll of Zerubbabel's return in Ezra 2:2ff.; Gill takes the verse as the caption of the list.
Clarke gives the whole chapter's compass in a sentence: genealogy, gathering at Ahava, the missing Levites, the fast, the charge of the treasure, and the safe arrival.

Keil and Delitzsch fix Gershom and Daniel as heads of the priestly houses of Phinehas and Ithamar (1 Chron. 6:3-4), noting this does not limit the priests to two (cf. Ezra 8:24), and Hattush as the shoot of David.
Gill warns that this Daniel is not the prophet (of Judah and the royal blood) but a priest of the line of Ithamar.
Clarke marks Gershom a descendant of Phinehas the son of Eleazar.

themes: priests and prince at the head

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch survey the twelve lay houses (ten identical in Hebrew and 1 Esdras), tie them to Zerubbabel's return (Ezra 2:3ff.), and resolve the doubled heading, reading Shechaniah as the wider clan of Zechariah of Parosh.
Clarke distinguishes three men named Shechaniah (here, v.6, Ezra 10:2); Wesley infers that though only males are counted, wives and little ones went too.
Gill distinguishes this Shechaniah from another of the same name.
Keil and Delitzsch place Pahath-moab among the twelve houses that also returned under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:6); Ellicott's rule joins the head Elihoenai to his wider family.
Matthew Henry reads the numbers as an honour-roll of the willing, some called at the third hour and some at the eleventh, the latecomers not rejected.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree a name has dropped from the Hebrew; the LXX restores 'of the sons of Zattu, Shechaniah' (cf. Ezra 2:8), an ordinary slip of transcription mended from the Greek.
Clarke keeps this second Shechaniah distinct from the others of the name.

Keil and Delitzsch reckon Elam among the ten houses identical in Hebrew and 1 Esdras, which had also returned under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:7); Ellicott joins the head Jeshaiah to his wider family and compares the earlier return (Ezra 2:2).
Matthew Henry honours the willing, however few; the seventy of Elam are eleventh-hour volunteers not rejected.

Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch note another name wanting, restored from the LXX as 'of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah' (cf. Ezra 2:10) — the same copyist's slip as at v.5, mended from the older Greek.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read 'the last sons' as the younger branches, the elder already reported in Ezra 2:13; Keil compares the idiom of 2 Samuel 19:11-12.
Wesley: the rest came before, so that now all the sons of Adonikam had returned, none left in Babylon.
Henry reports two readings — 'last' to their dispraise as reluctant enlisters, or (his own) to their honour, the whole family at last gathered home.

debates.question: Does 'the last sons of Adonikam' brand them as laggards or honour a completed return?

sides.position: a reproach — the last and most reluctant to enlist under Ezra
holders: some interpreters cited by Matthew Henry

sides.position: an honour — the whole house at last returned, none left behind

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch close the roll with Bigvai (cf. Ezra 2:14), note the 1 Esdras corruption of Uthai and Zabbud, and cast up the total: 1496 males and fifteen heads (Hebrew) against 1690 and thirteen (1 Esdras), priests and sons of David uncounted.
Matthew Henry gives the same Hebrew total, 1496, reading it as the honoured remnant that shook itself from the dust and followed Ezra home.

Keil and Delitzsch narrate Ezra's review and the discovery of no Levites; Ellicott fixes Ahava as river and town (nine days from Babylon, perhaps Hit), and grounds Ezra's anxiety in the mere 74 Levites who returned under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:40).
Clarke locates Ahava (Diava/Adiava in Adiabene, cf. the men of Ava, 2 Kings 17:24) and, with Wesley, stresses that priests were present but none who were simply Levites.
Gill connects the river Ahava with Adiabene.
Matthew Henry turns the Levites' absence into a reproach: where was the spirit of that sacred tribe, loath to leave their Babylonian synagogues for the gates of Zion?

Keil and Delitzsch carry the mission to its issue — 40 Levites and 220 Nethinim gathered through Iddo; Ellicott takes the two 'men of understanding' for teachers, perhaps priests, joined with nine chief men as the deputation.
Gill: nine men of chief note and two of good sense, three of them named Elnathan, all summoned from the camp.

themes: chief men and men of understanding

schools.summary: Ellicott sets Casiphia near Ahava, a Jewish colony under Iddo (himself a Nethinim, now chief), the 'ministers' including Levites and Nethinim; Gill (with Jarchi) makes it a place in or near Babylon, too near for the distant Caspian.
Clarke, with 'the most judicious commentators,' takes Casiphia for the Caspian mountains between Media and Hyrcania, where the Nethinim worked silver mines, keseph meaning silver.
Henry hears the silver in the name ('Silver Street') and pictures Iddo as president of a college of Levites, asked to send the juniors as ministers for God's house.

sides.position: a Jewish settlement in or near Babylon, within reach of Ahava
the distant Caspian mountains, a mining district named from its silver

themes: ministers for the house of God

schools.summary: Ellicott takes 'a man of understanding' as probably a proper name, Ishsekel (required by the 'and' before Sherebiah), and identifies Sherebiah the Levite with the expounder of Nehemiah 8:7.
Gill lays the success wholly to the good hand of God, favouring, protecting, and inclining the hearts of those approached.
Wesley: where ministers wanting are well supplied, ascribe it to the good hand of God qualifying, inclining, and opening a door.

Keil and Delitzsch place Hashabiah and Jeshaiah among the sons of Merari (twenty souls), and trace the Nethinim to the devoted Gibeonites (Josh. 9:21; Ezra 2:43), 'expressed by name' as men of note (cf. 1 Chron. 12:31).
Gill notes these were of the same Levitical division as Sherebiah.

Ellicott notes this is the sole record of David appointing the Nethinim, and reads 'expressed by name' as Iddo's forwarded name-list (not that all were famous), the relief ascribed to God's good hand; Keil takes 'by name' as marking men of note.
Gill weighs whether the Nethinim were the Gibeonites of Joshua confirmed by David, or a later addition, and defines their office as serving the Levites.

Keil and Delitzsch set the fast among Israel's ancient customs (Judg. 20:26; 1 Sam. 7:6; Joel 1:14; 2 Chron. 20:3) and gloss the 'right way' as a level, prosperous road (Ps. 112:7); Ellicott points to the desert enemy and reads 'substance' as chiefly the temple treasure.
Matthew Henry: Levites avail nothing unless God go with them; public mercies need public prayer; strangers on the road without a pillar of cloud commit their way to providence (Phil. 4:6).
Gill sets the fast just after the messengers' return; Wesley reads it as humiliation for sin and a plea for a safe journey.

Keil and Delitzsch expound the confession (God's hand for good on seekers, his power and wrath on forsakers); Ellicott reads the verse as looking back — Ezra's tribute to providence made seeking God the very condition of safety.
Clarke: Ezra could not consistently ask soldiers after magnifying God's power, lest the heathen think his religion vain; he cared more for God's glory than his own safety.
Gill: he might have had the guard for the asking, so great his favour with the king; the shame was for his testimony's sake.
Henry: he was ashamed to ask a convoy lest it make the court suspect God's power or his own confidence in it.

themes: God's hand for good and wrath

schools.summary: Matthew Henry: they besought God by joint prayer and he was entreated; never any who sought God in earnest sought him in vain — a set season of prayer is the best relief in danger.
Gill: they sought a good journey and preservation; Wesley: 'entreated' means God gave an assurance of his gracious answer.
Keil and Delitzsch pass to the next step, noting the difficult 'to Sherebiah, Hashabiah' — Levites of Merari, not priests, so not to be reckoned among the twelve chiefs of the priests.
Matthew Henry: prayer must be seconded with endeavour; holy things committed to God are also committed to faithful men (2 Tim. 2:2), and who so fit for holy charge as holy persons?
Ellicott construes 'to Sherebiah and Hashabiah': these two Levites with ten brethren were associated with an equal number of priests in the charge — twelve and twelve.
Gill infers from the number that more priests were present than the two named heads.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the offering as the freewill gifts of king, counsellors, lords, and the Israelites remaining in Babylon (cf. Ezra 7:15-16); Ellicott notes the gold and silver in bars and computes the enormous value.
Gill reads the weighing as Ezra's proof of integrity, an example and a security against any charge of embezzling.

Clarke corrects '100 talents' as the weight (not number) of the silver vessels, computes the whole above a million sterling, and takes the 'fine copper' for a factitious metal bright and durable as gold (cf. Corinthian brass).
Gill reckons the sterling values and records the tradition of 100 vessels each of a talent.
Keil and Delitzsch set the amounts in plain order and carry the count into the basins and copper vessels following.
Ellicott makes the 'thousand drams' darics (the basins worth over a thousand guineas) and the 'fine copper' probably the Roman orichalcum, highly valued.
Gill computes the golden basins by the weight of the Persian daric (Cumberland, Bernard).

Ellicott calls it a unique verse — consecrated treasures in consecrated hands, to be accounted for to the temple treasurers; Keil and Delitzsch: being holy themselves, they must keep the holy gifts as holy until they weigh them out at Jerusalem.
Gill: as the men were set apart to holy service, so the vessels to holy uses, not to be turned to common purpose.
Henry: who so fit to bear holy things as holy persons? — hearing Isaiah 52:11, 'be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD.'

themes: ye are holy, the vessels holy
a freewill offering to the Lord

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the terminus: watch and keep until weighed before the chief priests, Levites, and heads of fathers in the temple chambers; then the company departs on the twelfth day.
Henry expands 'watch': keep them together, by themselves, safely — a trust received by weight must be discharged by weight, fidelity the keeper's crown (cf. 2 Tim. 1:14).
Gill: watch and keep them, that they be not hurt nor diminished.
Keil and Delitzsch read 'took the weight' as receiving by weight what was delivered by weight, the transaction deliberately symmetrical.
Gill identifies the bearers as the twelve priests and twelve Levites named before.
Henry's governing thought: holy things committed to God are also committed to faithful men, who now shoulder them for the house of God.

themes: the keepers take up the charge
bound for the house of God

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reconcile the twelfth day with the first appointed (Ezra 7:9) by the three-day encampment, the search for Levites, and the fast; Ellicott sums 'the hand of our God was upon us' as the whole history of the journey.
Matthew Henry: the hand of God animated and preserved them from the enemies lurking like Amalek; common perils call for prayer at going out and thanks at coming home.
Gill dates the departure to Nisan, two days before the passover.

themes: the hand of God upon them

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the arrival on the first of the fifth month (three and a half months' journey) and the three days' quiet before the weighing (cf. Neh. 2:11); Ellicott takes the days for rest and private devotion.
Gill: a needful rest before any business was undertaken.

themes: rest and devotion before the sacred business

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch name the four receiving officers (two priests, two Levites) and the record by number and weight; Ellicott notes these same men recur in Nehemiah.
Gill marks the timing, the fourth day after arrival.
Ellicott: the count and weight written and laid up for security; Keil and Delitzsch: an authentic list drawn up at the delivery, all by number and weight.
Gill: delivered by tale and weight, exactly agreeing with what was received at Ahava.

Keil and Delitzsch read the offerings as gratitude for the restoration — twelve bullocks for the twelve tribes, twelve he-goats for sin (cf. Ezra 6:17), 96 (8x12) rams, 77 the intensified seven — the sin offering the basis of the burnt offering.

Clarke: a bullock for every tribe as if present, with individuals from all twelve though only Judah and Benjamin in force; Wesley reads 8x12 as the union of the two kingdoms, all twelve meeting at one altar, and stresses the atoning sin offering.
Gill identifies the worshippers as the children of the captivity newly come with Ezra.

Keil and Delitzsch: the royal decrees (Ezra 7:12-26) delivered to the satraps and governors beyond the river, who furthered people and house of God as Artaxerxes commanded; Ellicott distinguishes military satraps from civil pechahs and marks the order — God's things first, then Caesar's.
Clarke expounds 'the king's lieutenants' (achashdarpeney), a corrupted Persian word for satrap or viceroy.
Gill: the governors of Syria, Palestine, and Judea, on that side of the Euphrates.

themes: satraps and governors beyond the river
rendering to God then to Caesar
